claim: The actual read version is Neville Hogan's IEEE conference paper, Impedance Control: An Approach to Manipulation. It defines impedance control as commanding a physically realizable dynamic relation between conjugate endpoint motion and force variables, rather than commanding position or force alone. Because typical manipulation environments contain inertias and kinematic constraints and are therefore naturally described as admittances, the manipulator should present a complementary impedance. The paper gives direct Cartesian endpoint stiffness and damping implementations through forward kinematics and Jacobian-transpose force mapping, and an indirect mechanical route that uses kinematic redundancy to modulate endpoint mobility. It reports a real-time obstacle-avoidance and constrained-motion implementation, but does not provide a general contact-stability theorem, quantitative energetic-contact validation, or an adaptive or learning law for selecting impedance online.
claim_locator: Actual read version: IEEE conference proceedings paper, pages 304–313 in the supplied text; Abstract and Introduction; Implementation of Impedance Control; Impedance Control Without Feedback; Superposition of Impedances; Obstacle Avoidance; Summary and Conclusion; Appendix on generalized inertial systems and the mobility tensor; Figs. 1–3.
epistemic_status: Full-text reading of the user-accepted IEEE conference version only. Conceptual and mathematical statements are attributed to that version; implementation observations are author-reported. No claims unique to the separately referenced ASME Part II were imported.
problem_and_setting: Manipulation requires mechanical coupling and, in tasks such as drilling, grinding, bending, tool use, or contact transitions, non-negligible mechanical work is exchanged with the environment. Position, velocity, or force commands alone do not determine this exchange. The paper therefore reframes manipulation control around the behavior exposed at the endpoint interaction port, with effort and flow represented by force and motion or velocity. Free motion and pure kinematic constraints are treated as limiting cases within the broader dynamic-interaction problem.
method_or_mechanism: The causal classification distinguishes admittances, which accept force and produce motion, from impedances, which accept imposed motion and produce force; the distinction is fundamental for nonlinear systems. Since inertial and constrained environments can consistently be represented as admittances, physical compatibility motivates commanding the manipulator as an impedance. For direct software implementation, a desired endpoint stiffness F=K(X0−X) is mapped to actuator torque through forward kinematics X=L(θ) and virtual work, T=J(θ)^T F. A desired endpoint force–velocity relation is implemented analogously as T=J(θ)^T B(J(θ)ω). These laws need neither inverse kinematics nor Jacobian inversion and allow nonlinear endpoint relations. The paper also describes masking the manipulator's true dynamics to impose simpler apparent endpoint inertia, while emphasizing that physical inertia cannot be eliminated. As an indirect implementation, kinematic redundancy changes the configuration-dependent endpoint mobility W(θ)=J(θ)Y(θ)J(θ)^T, allowing mechanical modulation of apparent inertial behavior without relying solely on feedback. Component impedances, including target-attractive and obstacle-repulsive potential fields, are added because the coupled admittance sums applied forces.
content_summary: The paper introduces impedance control as a unified framework for free motion, kinematically constrained motion, and energetic interaction. Its core move is from controlling endpoint vectors to controlling the relation between endpoint force and motion. It argues that causal compatibility matters: a constrained inertial environment is naturally an admittance, so the robot should expose an impedance. Endpoint stiffness and damping can be imposed with commanded actuator torques, measured actuator positions and velocities, forward kinematics, and Jacobian-transpose mapping. This avoids solving inverse kinematics and supports redundant or nonsquare Jacobians without pseudoinverse control. Inertia requires separate care: simple stiffness and damping laws omit inertia, friction, and gravity, and no realizable controller can remove physical inertia, although apparent endpoint inertia may be modified through feedback or configuration. The endpoint mobility tensor provides a well-defined admittance-side representation even where an endpoint inertia inverse fails at singular configurations. The additive structure of component impedances permits target acquisition and obstacle avoidance to be designed separately and superimposed, including nonlinear repulsive fields. The authors report that one controller handled free-space avoidance of unpredictably moving objects and kinematically constrained motion in real time on a spherical-coordinate manipulator using one 8-bit, 2 MHz processor per axis. Adaptive control is discussed only as a complementary future strategy: fixed controlled impedance can handle rapid contact transitions while identification and adaptation optimize performance later.
synthesis_role: Foundational problem-definition and implementation card for the development of robotic impedance control. It establishes endpoint mechanical impedance as the controlled object, grounds it in port causality and energy exchange, and provides both controller-based and morphology/configuration-based implementation routes. It also marks the unresolved transition from manually specified impedance behavior to formally stable contact interaction and adaptive or learned online impedance selection.
development_link: This conference paper shifts robot manipulation from separate position and force control toward control of an endpoint force–motion relation. The Jacobian-transpose construction makes Cartesian stiffness and damping implementable without inverse kinematics, while mobility analysis links redundancy and configuration to apparent inertia. Superposition then turns impedance into a compositional command representation for target attraction, obstacle avoidance, and constrained motion. Later variable, adaptive, and learning impedance methods inherit this physically meaningful parameterization but must solve problems not resolved here: selecting impedance from changing observations, preserving stability during rapid contact transitions, accommodating model and sensing error, and validating energetic contact performance.

evidence.statement: For non-negligible dynamic interaction, controlling position, velocity, or force alone is inadequate because these vector commands do not determine the mechanical work exchanged with the environment.

A physical interaction port is described by effort and flow; admittances accept force and produce motion, whereas impedances accept motion and produce force, and this distinction is fundamental for nonlinear systems.

Because common manipulation environments contain inertia and kinematic constraints and can be written in admittance form, the paper argues that a coupled manipulator should present a complementary impedance.
A desired nonlinear Cartesian endpoint stiffness can be implemented as actuator torque T=J(θ)^T K(X0−L(θ)) using forward kinematics and virtual work, without inverse kinematics or Jacobian inversion.
A desired endpoint force–velocity relation can be implemented analogously through T=J(θ)^T B(J(θ)ω), again without Jacobian inversion.

The simple position- and velocity-dependent laws omit inertial, frictional, and gravitational dynamics; the paper states that physical inertia cannot be eliminated, although apparent endpoint inertia can be modified.

The endpoint mobility tensor W(θ)=J(θ)Y(θ)J(θ)^T maps endpoint momentum to velocity and, from rest, endpoint force to acceleration; redundant configurations can therefore modulate apparent endpoint inertia.
evidence.support_scope: Impedance Control Without Feedback and Appendix, Eqs. 8–10.

evidence.statement: Mobility remains computationally meaningful when singular kinematics make an endpoint inertia inverse nonexistent or infinite in some directions.
Target-attractive and obstacle-repulsive impedance components can be designed separately and superimposed, including nonlinear components, because the coupled admittance sums forces and impedances.
evidence.support_scope: Superposition of Impedances and Obstacle Avoidance; Fig. 2.

evidence.statement: The authors report real-time moving-obstacle avoidance and kinematically constrained motion with the same controller on a spherical-coordinate manipulator using 8-bit, 2 MHz processors, with successive obstacle-avoidance positions shown in Fig. 3.
Adaptive strategies are proposed as complementary: controlled impedance can cover rapid transitions while identification and adaptation subsequently optimize performance.

evidence_kind: Foundational physical-systems argument, endpoint controller derivations, generalized inertial and mobility analysis, qualitative implementation description, and author-reported real-time demonstration; no formal contact-stability proof, controlled comparative experiment, or learned impedance policy is presented in the actual read version.
boundary_conditions: The source actually read is the IEEE conference version identified in the file, not the separately referenced ASME Part II; conclusions are limited to content present in this conference text.
The direct Cartesian laws assume actuators capable of commanded force or torque, position or angle sensing, and a known forward kinematic map and Jacobian.
The displayed stiffness and damping mappings do not by themselves compensate inertia, friction, gravity, actuator limits, delays, or sensor noise.
The claim that inverse kinematics and Jacobian inversion are unnecessary applies to the presented impedance mappings, not to every planning, redundancy-resolution, or control objective.
The endpoint impedance/admittance causality argument is port- and direction-dependent; physical interconnection requires complementary causality along each interacting degree of freedom.
For nonlinear systems, impedance and admittance descriptions need not be interchangeable or globally invertible.
The mobility tensor is configuration dependent, and its endpoint inertia inverse may fail to exist at singular configurations even though mobility remains defined.
The superposition claim relies on an admittance that sums forces; it does not establish stability of every nonlinear, discontinuous, time-varying, or actively generated component impedance.
Potential-field simplification assumes position- and velocity-dependent fields with the stated integrability properties when a potential interpretation is used.
The obstacle-avoidance evidence is qualitative and limited to one spherical-coordinate manipulator and the hardware and computing arrangement described.

The reported controller demonstration concerns avoidance and constrained motion; the source does not report quantitative force tracking, energetic machining, impact robustness, or broad task benchmarks.
The text motivates rapid free-to-contact transitions but does not derive passivity, Lyapunov, or contact-stability conditions for switching or time-varying impedance.
Adaptation is discussed as a complement but no estimator, adaptive law, reinforcement-learning method, convergence result, or safety guarantee is supplied.
The paper allows intrinsic hardware mechanics and kinematic redundancy to implement impedance, so impedance control should not be equated exclusively with software feedback.
assumptions: The user-supplied text faithfully represents the accepted IEEE conference paper despite OCR artifacts in symbols and typography.

Equations are interpreted using standard notation: θ denotes actuator or joint coordinates, X endpoint position, J the configuration-dependent Jacobian, T actuator torque, Y joint-space mobility, and W endpoint mobility.
The environment-admittance premise is treated as the paper's general physical argument rather than an experimentally universal classification of all environments.
The reported obstacle-avoidance implementation is accepted as an author observation, not independently reproduced evidence.

The development link to adaptive and learning impedance is an historical and technical synthesis grounded in the paper's explicit adaptation discussion, not a claim that the paper implements learning.

reported: Position, velocity, or force control alone is inadequate for non-negligible dynamic interaction.
Simple endpoint stiffness and damping feedback omits inertial, frictional, and gravitational dynamics that may be non-negligible.
No physically realizable strategy can eliminate manipulator inertia, although its apparent endpoint effect can be modified.
For nonlinear systems, admittance and impedance are generally not interchangeable, and useful nonlinear impedance fields may have no inverse compliance representation.
At some linkage configurations, the endpoint inertia tensor does not exist because endpoint mobility has zero eigenvalues.
Continuous environmental identification and controller restructuring may be too slow for abrupt free-motion-to-contact transitions.
inferred: Without explicit passivity or stability constraints, superimposing nonlinear or time-varying impedance components may produce unsafe energy injection or unstable contact despite the compositional force construction.

The direct implementation's dependence on kinematic and dynamic knowledge can make realized endpoint impedance deviate from the command under model error, delay, saturation, friction, or unmodeled compliance.
A fixed or manually commanded impedance cannot by itself determine task-optimal stiffness, damping, or inertia across changing contacts, motivating later adaptive and learning-based gain selection.
Avoiding inverse kinematics does not resolve redundancy objectives, joint limits, singularity avoidance, or global workspace feasibility.
The qualitative obstacle-avoidance demonstration does not establish robustness to arbitrary obstacle speed, sensing error, contact, or computational latency.
Treating controlled impedance as a buffer for adaptation identifies a promising architecture but leaves the stability of simultaneous online adaptation and physical interaction unresolved.
